c.tagline: Africa's Atlantic capital of cobbled streets and hilltop sea views.

taxi.fareNote: Meters are rarely used; agree the fare (often a per-zone flat rate) with the driver before departure. Shared taxis running set routes are common and cheaper than private hire.

emergency.note: Fire/rescue: 131. National Civil Protection hotline: 8001112. Medical facilities are limited; serious cases are sometimes evacuated to Portugal.

avoid.reason: Avoid peripheral districts such as Safende, Achadinha and Vila Nova, especially after dark, due to gang-related street crime.
Watch for pickpockets in Sucupira market and on the Plateau, and skip deserted beaches or unlit streets at night.

hood_desc: The compact hilltop historic core of Praia with colonial-era buildings, the main square, a pedestrian shopping street and government offices; best for travelers who want to walk to sights, markets and transit without a car.

An upscale seaside district just below the Plateau with the city's most popular beach and promenade plus Praia's most polished mid-range and business hotels; suits visitors who want ocean views within a short walk of downtown.

A large, leafy residential and commercial neighborhood favored by expats, NGO and government workers, with supermarkets, banks and several hotels; suits longer-stay visitors wanting a quieter, local residential base.

An affluent commercial and residential zone with newer shopping centers, embassies and office towers alongside business-oriented hotels; suits business travelers and those wanting modern conveniences a short drive from the center.

A working, low-key coastal district beside Gamboa beach with fishing boats on the sand and a mix of budget guesthouses and beachfront hotels; suits budget travelers wanting an authentic beach vibe close to downtown.

water.note: Despite treated desalinated supply, aging pipes and inconsistent delivery mean bottled water is safest.

transit.pay: Public buses and shared vans (hiace/Yasa) are paid in cash to the driver or conductor in escudos; there is no rechargeable transit card. Fares are flat within the city regardless of distance ridden.
transit.hours: Buses and shared vans generally run roughly 6:00-20:00; service thins out sharply after dark, so most nighttime trips are made by taxi.
transit.note: There is no metro, tram or train; getting around is by minibus/shared van, taxi, or on foot within neighborhoods like the Plateau.

bus: Aluguer/Hiace shared vans to other towns on Santiago island
ferry: Inter-island ferries (CV Interilhas and others) from Porto da Praia to Fogo, Brava, Maio and other islands

transit.m: Public bus into city center (30-40 min)

tip.r: Tipping is not obligatory; rounding up the bill or leaving 5-10% at sit-down restaurants in tourist areas is appreciated but not expected elsewhere.

food.name: Cachupa
food.desc: Cabo Verde's national stew: hominy corn and beans slow-cooked with cassava, pumpkin and whatever fish or pork is around, until thick and smoky.

places.name: Cafe Sofia
places.note: Known for breakfast cachupa refogada, fried up with egg and sausage.

places.name: Quintal da Musica
places.note: Cape Verdean kitchen with nightly live morna and coladeira.

places.name: Mercado Municipal da Praia
places.note: Market food counters ladle out cachupa rica at local prices from mid-morning.

food.name: Pastel com diabo dentro
food.desc: Devil-inside pastry: a sweet-potato-and-cornmeal shell wrapped around spicy tuna and onion, then deep-fried until blistered.

places.name: Mercado de Sucupira
places.note: The city's huge open market; fry stalls turn these out hot all day.

places.name: Mercado Municipal da Praia

places.name: Plateau street stalls
places.note: From about 5pm the streets fill with the smell of frying cornmeal.

food.name: Buzio guisado (stewed sea snails)
food.desc: Large ocean snails prised from their shells and stewed with onion, tomato, garlic and piri-piri; a classic Santiago bar snack with a cold beer.

places.name: Quintal da Musica
places.note: Cape Verdean petiscos including shellfish, served with live music.

places.name: Quebra Canela beach bars
places.note: Seafront shacks serving buzio and grilled fish straight off the beach.

places.name: Mercado Municipal da Praia
places.note: Buy them fresh at the fish hall or eat them cooked at the counters.

food.name: Grilled tuna and lagostim
food.desc: Thick steaks of Atlantic tuna or wahoo grilled over charcoal, plus local spiny lobster, both served simply with lime, rice and beans.

places.name: Cafe Sofia
places.note: Seafood specialities including grilled prawns and marinated octopus.

places.name: Quebra Canela beach bars
places.note: Grills right on the sand, cooking whatever the boats landed that morning.

places.name: Prainha waterfront restaurants
places.note: Hotel and seafront kitchens on the bay doing the pricier grilled-fish version.

food.name: Djagacida
food.desc: Santiago's one-pot rice dish, chicken cooked down with rice, onions and tomato until the grains take on all the fat and colour.

places.name: Quintal da Musica
places.note: Reliable place to find the island's home-style rice dishes on the menu.

places.name: Mercado de Sucupira
places.note: Market canteens serve the day's rice dish as a set lunch.

places.name: Achada Santo Antonio local restaurants
places.note: Residential quarter where the small dining rooms cook for regulars, not tourists.

food.name: Cuscuz and doce de papaia
food.desc: Steamed cornmeal cake eaten warm with mel de cana sugarcane honey at breakfast, and the sweet papaya preserve served after dinner.

places.name: Mercado Municipal da Praia
places.note: Women sell steamed cuscuz from cloth-covered baskets in the morning.

places.name: Cafe Sofia
places.note: Cafe on the square doing pancakes, pastries and Cape Verdean breakfast plates.

places.name: Mercado de Sucupira
places.note: Stalls sell cane honey, papaya sweets and coconut doces to take away.

food.name: Grogue
food.desc: Cabo Verde's cane spirit, distilled in copper stills in the Santiago valleys and drunk neat as a small measure before or after eating.

places.name: Mercado de Sucupira
places.note: Stalls sell small bottles of village grogue from the island's distilleries.

places.name: Cidade Velha trapiches
places.note: The historic old capital where the sugarcane presses and stills still work.

places.name: Quintal da Musica
places.note: Grogue poured by the glass with the evening music sessions.

food.name: Ponche
food.desc: Grogue softened with mel de cana cane honey and lemon, sometimes coconut or passionfruit; the sweet, dangerous house cocktail of the islands.

places.name: Quintal da Musica
places.note: Classic spot to drink ponche while the band plays morna and funana.

places.name: Quebra Canela beach bars
places.note: Sunset ponche and caipirinha-style grogue drinks by the water.

places.name: Mercado de Sucupira
places.note: Bottled homemade ponche in several flavours sold from market stalls.

landmarks: Fortaleza Real de São Filipe
This imposing 16th-century Portuguese fortress overlooks Cidade Velha and the Atlantic, standing as a powerful reminder of Cape Verde's colonial and trade history.
Pelourinho of Cidade Velha
This weathered marble whipping post in the UNESCO-listed old town square is a somber but essential landmark tied to the history of the slave trade.
Sé Catedral Ruins
The atmospheric ruins of Africa's oldest colonial cathedral, built in the 1600s, rise dramatically against the sky in the historic town of Cidade Velha.
Platô (Plateau District)
Praia's historic hilltop center features colorful colonial buildings, plazas, and government offices, forming the picturesque heart of the capital city.
Presidential Palace
This elegant colonial-era mansion, once the governor's residence, now serves as the official seat of Cape Verde's president overlooking the ocean.
National Assembly Building
The seat of Cape Verde's parliament is a notable modern landmark in Praia, symbolizing the nation's democratic institutions and civic pride.
Quebra Canela Beach
A popular crescent of golden sand near downtown Praia, protected by a small headland, making it a favorite spot for swimming and relaxing.
Ethnographic Museum of Praia
Housed in a charming plateau building, this museum showcases traditional Cape Verdean crafts, instruments, and daily-life artifacts reflecting the islands' Creole culture.
Nossa Senhora da Graça Church
This graceful whitewashed church is a beloved architectural landmark in the Plateau district, admired for its simple colonial facade and central location.
Praia Cityscape
Perched on volcanic cliffs above the Atlantic, Praia's dramatic aerial panorama of pastel buildings and coastline is a favorite subject for photographers.

train.note: Cabo Verde has no railways on any island.

bus.note: As an island nation, Cabo Verde has no international bus routes and no national coach company. Get around Santiago and between towns by shared 'aluguer' minibuses (Toyota Hiace). International travel is by air (Praia's Nelson Mandela International Airport) or by inter-island ferry.

ferry.note: No international passenger ferries - every sea link is domestic. CV Interilhas (https://www.cvinterilhas.cv/) sails from Praia to Fogo (Sao Filipe), Brava, Maio and other islands; check current timetables and weather, as crossings can be rough and cancelled.

half.name: Igreja de Nossa Senhora do Rosário
half.blurb: Ruined church in Cidade Velha, about 30 minutes away, is considered the oldest colonial church still standing in sub-Saharan Africa.

half.name: Serra da Malagueta
half.blurb: Mountain nature reserve about an hour north rises over 1,000 meters and holds trails through cloud-forest vegetation found nowhere else on the islands.

half.name: Tarrafal
half.blurb: Beach town on the island's north coast, about 90 minutes away, holds a former political prison used under Portuguese colonial rule.

half.name: São Jorge dos Órgãos
half.blurb: Village about 40 minutes away holds Cabo Verde's national botanical garden, home to hundreds of native and imported plant species.
